lessons.title: Atoms, Elements and the Development of the Atomic Model
lessons.description: From Dalton's solid spheres to Chadwick's neutron — how evidence changed our model of the atom.
lessons.content_html:
Atoms, Elements and Compounds

All matter is made of tiny particles called atoms. An element is a pure substance containing only one type of atom — for example, copper contains only copper atoms and chlorine contains only chlorine atoms. When atoms of different elements join together chemically, they form a compound. In a compound, the atoms are held by chemical bonds and can only be separated by chemical reactions. Mixtures, by contrast, contain more than one substance not chemically bonded, and can be separated by physical means.

Key Fact

All matter is made of atoms. Elements contain only one type of atom. Compounds contain atoms of two or more different elements chemically bonded together in fixed proportions. Atoms are neither created nor destroyed in chemical reactions.

Structure of the Atom

The atom has a central nucleus containing protons (positively charged) and neutrons (no charge). Electrons (negatively charged) orbit the nucleus in shells (energy levels). In a neutral atom, the number of protons equals the number of electrons, so the charges balance.

The relative masses and charges of the three subatomic particles are:

  • Proton: relative mass 1, charge +1.
  • Neutron: relative mass 1, charge 0.
  • Electron: relative mass approximately 0 (very small compared to protons and neutrons), charge −1.

Two numbers describe every atom. The atomic number (proton number) is the number of protons in the nucleus and determines which element the atom is. The mass number is the total number of protons plus neutrons. The number of neutrons in a neutral atom = mass number − atomic number.

Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. For example, carbon-12 has 6 protons and 6 neutrons, while carbon-14 has 6 protons and 8 neutrons. Both are carbon because they have atomic number 6. Isotopes of an element have the same chemical properties (same electron arrangement) but different physical properties (different masses).

Because naturally occurring elements often consist of a mixture of isotopes, the relative atomic mass (Aᵣ) is calculated as a weighted mean. For example, chlorine has two isotopes: chlorine-35 (about 75% abundant) and chlorine-37 (about 25% abundant). Its relative atomic mass is approximately: $$A_r = \frac{(75 \times 35) + (25 \times 37)}{100} = \frac{2625 + 925}{100} = 35.5$$

Key Fact

Isotopes have the same proton number (atomic number) but different neutron numbers (different mass numbers). Relative atomic mass is the weighted mean mass, taking account of the abundance of each isotope. Isotopes have identical chemistry because they have the same electron arrangement.

The Development of the Atomic Model

Our model of the atom has changed repeatedly as new experimental evidence came to light. This history shows how scientific models are provisional — they are the best explanation of available evidence and are revised when new evidence demands it.

1803–1808

Dalton’s Atomic Theory

John Dalton proposed that all matter was made of tiny indivisible spheres called atoms. A key claim of Dalton’s model was that all atoms of a given element are identical in mass and properties, and that atoms of different elements differ in mass. He also proposed that atoms cannot be created or destroyed in chemical reactions and that compounds are formed by the combination of atoms in fixed whole-number ratios. The existence of isotopes later showed that not all atoms of an element are identical in mass — refining Dalton’s claim.

1897

Thomson — Discovery of the Electron and the ‘Plum Pudding’ Model

J.J. Thomson discovered the electron and concluded that atoms contained smaller, negatively charged particles. He proposed the ‘plum pudding’ model: the atom is a diffuse sphere of positive charge with electrons embedded in it like plums in a pudding. This model retained the idea that the atom is a solid structure but revealed that atoms have internal structure.

1909–1911

Rutherford — the Gold Foil Experiment

Ernest Rutherford, working with Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden, fired alpha particles at a thin sheet of gold foil. Most particles passed straight through, but a small number were deflected at large angles, and a very few bounced almost straight back. This was inconsistent with the plum pudding model. Rutherford concluded that most of the mass of an atom is concentrated in a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus, with a large amount of empty space around it. Electrons orbit the nucleus at a distance.

1913

Bohr — Electrons in Shells

Niels Bohr proposed that electrons orbit the nucleus in specific, fixed energy levels (shells) rather than anywhere in the space around the nucleus. This explained the discrete emission spectra of elements. Each shell can hold a set number of electrons (the first holds up to 2, the second up to 8, and so on).

1932

Chadwick — Discovery of the Neutron

James Chadwick discovered the neutron, confirming that the nucleus contains uncharged particles as well as protons. This explained why atoms are heavier than the number of protons alone would suggest, and why isotopes of the same element exist.

The plum pudding model predicted that all alpha particles would be deflected only slightly by the diffuse positive charge. Rutherford’s gold foil experiment showed that a small fraction bounced back sharply — something the plum pudding model could not explain. A new model was needed: the nuclear model, in which almost all the mass and all the positive charge are concentrated in a tiny nucleus at the centre of a largely empty atom. Rutherford’s result is a classic example of how a single experiment can overturn an established model in science.
lessons.exam_tip_html: The gold foil experiment comes up regularly — be ready to explain the result (most particles pass through; a small number are deflected; very few bounce back) and connect each observation to the nuclear model (mostly empty space; positively charged nucleus; dense, concentrated nucleus). For isotope questions, remember: same element = same atomic number = same proton number. For relative atomic mass calculations, always show your working and check your weighted mean makes sense (it should lie between the two isotope masses).
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Atoms consist of a nucleus (protons + neutrons) surrounded by electrons in shells. Atomic number = protons; mass number = protons + neutrons; neutrons = mass number − atomic number.
  • Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same proton number but different neutron numbers. Relative atomic mass is the weighted mean mass, accounting for isotope abundance.
  • The atomic model evolved: Dalton (solid spheres) → Thomson (plum pudding) → Rutherford (nuclear model from gold foil experiment, 1909–1911) → Bohr (electrons in shells, 1913) → Chadwick (neutron, 1932).

lessons.title: The Periodic Table and Mendeleev
lessons.description: How Mendeleev arranged the elements, electronic configuration, and trends in Groups 0, 1 and 7.
lessons.content_html:
How Mendeleev Organised the Elements

Before atomic structure was understood, chemists tried to organise elements by their properties. Dmitri Mendeleev (1834–1907) published his periodic table in 1869. He arranged elements in order of atomic weight and grouped elements with similar chemical properties in the same column. Crucially, he left gaps where no known element fitted the pattern, predicting that new elements would be discovered to fill them. When elements such as gallium and germanium were later discovered and their properties closely matched his predictions, the scientific community accepted his table.

Mendeleev also swapped the positions of some elements so that their chemical properties aligned with their group, even if this meant they were not in strict order of atomic weight. This was a bold move, but it was vindicated when atomic numbers (rather than atomic weights) were later found to be the true basis for ordering the elements.

Key Fact

Mendeleev’s table (1869) organised elements by atomic weight, grouped similar properties in columns, and left gaps for undiscovered elements. The accurate prediction of the properties of those missing elements was key evidence that the table was correct.

The Modern Periodic Table

The modern periodic table arranges all known elements in order of atomic number (number of protons). Elements in the same vertical column share the same group. Elements in the same horizontal row share the same period. Metals are on the left and in the centre of the table; non-metals are on the right.

Electronic configuration determines chemical behaviour. The first electron shell holds up to 2 electrons; the second and third each hold up to 8. You can write the electronic configuration of an atom from its atomic number — for example, sodium (atomic number 11) is written as 2, 8, 1 (2 electrons in shell 1; 8 in shell 2; 1 in shell 3). Elements in the same group have the same number of electrons in their outermost shell, which is why they share similar chemical properties.

Write the electronic configuration of chlorine (atomic number 17). Fill shells in order: shell 1 takes 2 electrons (2 used, 15 remaining); shell 2 takes 8 (10 used, 7 remaining); shell 3 takes the remaining 7. Electronic configuration of chlorine: 2, 8, 7. Because chlorine has 7 outer electrons, it is in Group 7 and behaves as a halogen. From an atom’s electronic configuration, you can identify its group (= number of outer electrons, for groups 1–7) and period (= number of shells).

Group 0 — The Noble Gases

The noble gases (helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon, radon) have full outer electron shells. This makes them extremely stable and chemically unreactive — they do not normally form compounds. Going down Group 0, the boiling points increase (from −269°C for helium to −62°C for radon) because the atoms become larger, with stronger intermolecular forces between them.

Group 1 — The Alkali Metals

The alkali metals (Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs, Fr) each have one electron in their outer shell. They react with water to produce a metal hydroxide and hydrogen gas — for example: $$2Na + 2H_2O \rightarrow 2NaOH + H_2$$

Going down Group 1, reactivity increases. This is because the outer electron is in a shell further from the nucleus, so the electrostatic attraction between the nucleus and the outer electron is weaker. The outer electron is more easily lost, making the metal more reactive. Going down the group, melting and boiling points decrease, and density generally increases.

Key Fact

Group 1 metals have one outer electron and react vigorously with water. Reactivity increases down the group because the outer electron is further from the nucleus and more easily lost. This is the opposite trend to Group 7.

Group 7 — The Halogens

The halogens (F, Cl, Br, I, At) have seven electrons in their outer shell. They exist as diatomic molecules (e.g. Cl2, Br2). Going down Group 7, reactivity decreases. This is because the outer shell is further from the nucleus, so the atom has a weaker pull on an incoming electron from a reaction partner — it is harder to gain the extra electron needed to complete the outer shell.

Physical state at room temperature changes down the group: fluorine is a pale yellow gas; chlorine is a yellow-green gas; bromine is an orange liquid; iodine is a grey-black solid. Boiling points increase down the group.

A more reactive halogen can displace a less reactive halogen from a solution of its salt. For example, chlorine displaces bromine from potassium bromide solution: $$Cl_2 + 2KBr \rightarrow 2KCl + Br_2$$ The solution turns orange as bromine is formed. This reaction confirms the reactivity order: fluorine > chlorine > bromine > iodine. Iodine cannot displace chlorine from a chloride solution because iodine is less reactive than chlorine.

The transition metals occupy the central block of the periodic table. Compared with Group 1 metals they are much less reactive, have higher melting points, are harder and denser, and typically form coloured compounds. Many transition metals and their compounds act as catalysts — for example, iron is used as the catalyst in the industrial Haber process for making ammonia. Transition metals can form ions with different charges (e.g. iron can form Fe2+ and Fe3+).

Key Fact

Group 7 reactivity decreases down the group because the outer shell is further from the nucleus, making it harder for the atom to attract and gain an electron. This is the opposite of Group 1, where losing one electron gets easier down the group.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Two classic errors to avoid in periodic table questions: (1) saying “reactivity increases down Group 7” — it decreases because it becomes harder to gain an electron; (2) confusing groups and periods — groups are vertical columns (same outer electrons), periods are horizontal rows (same number of shells). For displacement reactions, you must state which halogen is more reactive and explain why the displacement does (or does not) occur. Show the word equation or symbol equation for full marks on 3-mark calculation questions about electronic configurations.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Dmitri Mendeleev (1834–1907) organised elements by atomic weight, left gaps for undiscovered elements and grouped similar properties in columns — his predictions of missing elements confirmed his table. The modern table uses atomic number.
  • Electronic configuration follows the pattern 2, 8, 8 ... for the first three shells. Group number = outer electrons (groups 1–7). Group 0 elements have full outer shells and are unreactive noble gases.
  • Group 1 reactivity increases down the group (outer electron further from nucleus, more easily lost). Group 7 reactivity decreases down the group (harder to gain an electron from a more distant outer shell). A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive one from its salt solution.

lessons.title: Ionic, Covalent and Metallic Bonding
lessons.description: How ions form, electron transfer and sharing, dot-and-cross diagrams and metallic delocalised electrons.
lessons.content_html:
Ionic Bonding

When a metal reacts with a non-metal, electrons are transferred from the metal atom to the non-metal atom. The metal atom loses one or more electrons to form a positive ion (cation), and the non-metal atom gains those electrons to become a negative ion (anion). Both ions then have full outer electron shells and are stable.

The strong electrostatic attraction between the oppositely charged ions is called an ionic bond. In sodium chloride (NaCl), sodium loses one electron to become \(Na^+\) and chlorine gains one electron to become \(Cl^-\). The resulting ions pack together in a regular three-dimensional arrangement called a giant ionic lattice.

Key Fact

Ionic bonding: metal atoms lose electrons (form positive ions) and non-metal atoms gain electrons (form negative ions). Strong electrostatic attraction between the opposite charges holds ions together in a giant ionic lattice.

Naming Ionic Compounds

The name of an ionic compound gives useful information about which ions are present. When a metal combines with a non-metal element only, the non-metal ion takes an -ide ending — for example, sodium chloride, magnesium oxide, potassium iodide. When the compound contains oxygen as part of a polyatomic ion, it usually takes an -ate ending — for example, sodium sulfate, copper(II) nitrate, calcium carbonate. Recognising these endings tells you instantly whether a simple or complex ion is involved.

Dot-and-cross diagrams show only the outer shell electrons. Use dots for one atom and crosses for the other. For sodium chloride:

  • Draw Na with one outer electron (dot). Draw Cl with seven outer electrons (crosses).
  • Show the dot crossing into Cl's outer shell, so Cl now has eight electrons. Draw square brackets around each ion and write the charge outside: \([Na]^+\) and \([Cl]^-\).

For magnesium oxide, Mg loses two electrons (2,8 → 2,8, 0 becomes \(Mg^{2+}\)) and oxygen gains two (2,6 → 2,8, becomes \(O^{2-}\)).

Covalent Bonding

When non-metals bond with other non-metals, atoms share pairs of electrons rather than transferring them. Each shared pair of electrons is a covalent bond. Both atoms count the shared pair as part of their own outer shell, so both achieve a full, stable electron configuration.

Common examples:

  • \(H_2\) — a single covalent bond (one shared pair).
  • \(O_2\) — a double covalent bond (\(O=O\), two shared pairs).
  • \(H_2O\) — two single covalent bonds (oxygen bonds to two hydrogen atoms).
  • \(CH_4\) — four single covalent bonds (carbon bonds to four hydrogen atoms).
  • \(NH_3\) — three single covalent bonds plus one lone pair on nitrogen.

For water (\(H_2O\)): draw oxygen in the centre with six outer-shell electrons. Draw a hydrogen on each side with one electron. Show one dot from O and one cross from each H overlapping in a shared pair. Each H now has a full shell of two; oxygen has a full shell of eight.

For methane (\(CH_4\)): carbon has four outer electrons. Each of the four hydrogen atoms contributes one electron. Show four shared pairs around carbon, giving it eight; each hydrogen has two.

Only draw outer-shell electrons. Never add electrons that aren't there or remove electrons to make the diagram look neater — the total electron count must balance.

Metallic Bonding

In metals, the outer electrons leave their parent atoms and become delocalised electrons — free to move throughout the entire metal structure. What remains are positive metal ions. The metallic bond is the strong electrostatic attraction between these positive ions and the surrounding sea of electrons.

Key Fact

Metallic bonding: positive metal ions in a lattice surrounded by a sea of delocalised electrons. The electrons carry charge → metals conduct electricity. Layers of ions can slide over each other → metals are malleable and ductile.

Ionic: electrons transferred, metal + non-metal, giant ionic lattice, high melting point, conducts when molten or dissolved.

Covalent: electrons shared, non-metal + non-metal, simple molecules (low m.p.) or giant covalent (very high m.p.), mostly poor conductors.

Metallic: delocalised electrons, metal atoms only, giant metallic lattice, good conductors, malleable, generally high melting points (though mercury is liquid at room temperature).

The key exam skill is justifying properties from structure: ionic compounds have high melting points because many strong electrostatic attractions must be overcome simultaneously. Simple covalent molecules like water have low boiling points because intermolecular forces, not covalent bonds, are broken during boiling. Giant covalent structures like diamond and silicon dioxide have very high melting points because many strong covalent bonds must be broken throughout the entire lattice.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For 4-mark explain questions on bonding, always link structure to property with a causal 'because' — for example: 'ionic compounds have high melting points because there are strong electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions acting in all directions, so a large amount of energy is needed to overcome them.' One mark for the claim, one for the scientific reason. For dot-and-cross diagrams, examiners check that (1) only outer shells are shown, (2) shared pairs sit in an overlap between atoms for covalent or are fully transferred with charges for ionic, and (3) the electron count balances. Remember: -ide endings indicate a binary ionic compound (two elements only); -ate endings indicate a polyatomic ion containing oxygen.

Key Takeaways

  • Ionic bonding: electrons transfer from metal to non-metal, forming oppositely charged ions held in a giant lattice by electrostatic attraction. -ide compounds contain a simple non-metal ion; -ate compounds contain an oxygen-bearing polyatomic ion.
  • Covalent bonding: non-metals share electron pairs so each atom achieves a full outer shell. Dot-and-cross diagrams show only outer shell electrons, with shared pairs in the overlap region.
  • Metallic bonding: delocalised electrons move freely between positive metal ions, making metals good conductors of electricity and heat and giving them the malleability to be shaped.

lessons.title: Structure, Properties and Carbon Allotropes
lessons.description: Giant ionic lattices, simple molecules, giant covalent structures, graphite, diamond, fullerenes and graphene.
lessons.content_html:
Properties of Ionic Compounds

Ionic compounds form giant ionic lattices. The strong electrostatic forces between the ions act in all directions, which gives ionic compounds a characteristic set of properties:

  • High melting and boiling points — a large amount of energy is needed to overcome the many strong bonds acting throughout the lattice.
  • Conduct electricity when molten or dissolved in water — the ions are then free to move and carry charge. They do not conduct when solid because the ions are fixed in position.
  • Brittle — if an external force shifts one layer of ions, identical charges align and repel each other strongly, shattering the crystal.
Key Fact

Ionic compounds: high melting points (strong forces in all directions), conduct when molten or dissolved (ions free to move), do not conduct when solid (ions fixed), brittle (layers shift → repulsion).

Properties of Simple Molecular Substances

Simple molecules (e.g. \(H_2O\), \(CO_2\), \(O_2\)) have strong covalent bonds within the molecule but weak intermolecular forces between molecules. This gives them:

  • Low melting and boiling points — little energy is needed to overcome the weak intermolecular forces (not the covalent bonds themselves).
  • Do not conduct electricity — no free electrons or ions to carry charge.

As molecules get larger, their intermolecular forces become stronger, so boiling points increase with molecular size. This is why large hydrocarbons are liquid or solid at room temperature while small ones (e.g. methane) are gases.

Key Fact

When a simple molecular substance melts or boils, the weak intermolecular forces are overcome — the strong covalent bonds within molecules remain intact. This explains why simple molecules have low melting points despite having strong internal bonds.

Giant Covalent Structures

Giant covalent structures have millions of atoms connected by covalent bonds in a continuous network. They have very high melting points because many strong covalent bonds must be broken to separate the atoms. Examples include diamond, graphite and silicon dioxide.

In diamond, each carbon atom forms four covalent bonds arranged in a rigid tetrahedral pattern. This gives diamond:

  • Extreme hardness — the rigid lattice resists deformation.
  • A very high melting point — all four bonds per atom must be broken.
  • No electrical conductivity — all four outer electrons are used in bonding, leaving none free to carry charge.

In graphite, each carbon atom bonds to three others in flat hexagonal layers. The fourth outer electron from each carbon becomes delocalised — free to move along the layers, allowing graphite to conduct electricity. The layers are held together only by weak intermolecular forces, so they slide easily over one another, making graphite soft and slippery — useful as a lubricant and in pencil leads.

Graphene, Fullerenes and Carbon Nanotubes

Graphene is a single layer of graphite: a one-atom-thick sheet of hexagonally arranged carbon atoms. Scientists Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov isolated it at the University of Manchester in 2004, work for which they received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2010. Graphene is extraordinarily strong relative to its mass and is an excellent conductor of electricity and heat.

Fullerenes are carbon molecules shaped as hollow spheres or tubes. Buckminsterfullerene (\(C_{60}\)) — 60 carbon atoms arranged like a football — was first made in 1985 by Harold Kroto, Robert Curl and Richard Smalley, who were awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1996.

Carbon nanotubes are cylindrical fullerenes with remarkable tensile strength and electrical conductivity. They are used in electronics and as reinforcing agents in composite materials.

Key Fact

Diamond: 4 bonds per carbon, rigid, hard, no conductivity. Graphite: 3 bonds per carbon + 1 delocalised electron, layers slide, conducts electricity. Graphene: single graphite layer — isolated 2004, strongest known material per unit mass.

Polymers are very large molecules made from many repeating units called monomers, joined by covalent bonds. Examples include poly(ethene) and poly(propene). The long tangled chains experience stronger intermolecular forces than simple molecules, so polymers are solid at room temperature. They do not conduct electricity and generally have moderate melting points depending on chain length and degree of cross-linking.

When comparing allotropes in the exam, always link structure to property: graphite conducts because delocalised electrons move between layers, whereas diamond does not because all four outer electrons are covalently bonded. Fullerenes and graphene are studied for nanotechnology applications — fullerene cages can carry drug molecules, while graphene's exceptional strength comes from the hexagonal arrangement of carbon atoms in a single layer.
lessons.exam_tip_html: A very common error on 6-mark questions: students say 'covalent bonds break when graphite or diamond melts'. For graphite, the weak intermolecular forces between layers are overcome on melting, not the covalent bonds — this is why graphite still has a very high melting point. For simple molecules, the intermolecular forces are overcome but the covalent bonds within the molecule stay intact. Always name the type of force being overcome, not just 'bonds'. For graphene/fullerenes questions, examiners want the year 1985 (buckminsterfullerene) and 2004 (graphene isolation) — but if unsure, paraphrase: 'discovered in the late twentieth century'.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Ionic compounds form giant lattices — high melting points, conduct when molten or dissolved, brittle. Simple molecular substances have low melting points because only weak intermolecular forces need overcoming.
  • Giant covalent structures (diamond, graphite, graphene) have very high melting points. Diamond is the hardest natural material; graphite conducts electricity due to delocalised electrons and has layers that slide.
  • Graphene (isolated 2004) is a single graphite layer — extremely strong and conductive. Fullerenes include C₆₀ (buckminsterfullerene, made 1985) and carbon nanotubes, with applications in electronics and materials science.

lessons.title: Quantitative Chemistry: Moles, Mass and Yield
lessons.description: Avogadro's number, calculating moles from mass, balanced equations, percentage yield and atom economy.
lessons.content_html:
What Is a Mole?

A mole is the chemist's counting unit. Just as a dozen always means 12, one mole always contains \(6.02 \times 10^{23}\) particles — whether those particles are atoms, molecules or ions. This enormous number is called Avogadro's constant (\(N_A\)).

The key link between moles and mass is the molar mass. For any element, the molar mass in grams equals its relative atomic mass (\(A_r\)). For compounds, add up the \(A_r\) values of all the atoms in the formula to get the relative formula mass (\(M_r\)).

Key Fact

\[\text{moles} = \frac{\text{mass (g)}}{\text{molar mass (g/mol)}}\] One mole of any element has a mass equal to its relative atomic mass in grams. For CO₂: \(M_r = 12 + (2 \times 16) = 44\,\text{g/mol}\).

Q: Calculate the number of moles in 22 g of carbon dioxide (\(CO_2\), \(M_r = 44\)).

Step 1 — Find \(M_r\): \(12 + (2 \times 16) = 44\,\text{g/mol}\).

Step 2 — Apply the formula: \(\text{moles} = \frac{22}{44} = 0.5\,\text{mol}\).

Q: What mass of sodium hydroxide (NaOH, \(M_r = 40\)) contains 0.25 mol?

Rearrange: \(\text{mass} = \text{moles} \times M_r = 0.25 \times 40 = 10\,\text{g}\).

Using Moles in Balanced Equations

A balanced chemical equation shows the molar ratio of reactants to products. For example:

$$2\,Mg + O_2 \rightarrow 2\,MgO$$

The numbers in front (coefficients) tell you that 2 moles of magnesium react with 1 mole of oxygen to produce 2 moles of magnesium oxide. To find the mass of a product from a known mass of reactant: (1) calculate moles of reactant, (2) use the ratio to find moles of product, (3) convert moles of product to mass.

Q: What mass of MgO is produced when 12 g of Mg burns completely? (\(A_r\): Mg = 24, O = 16)

Step 1 — Moles of Mg: \(\frac{12}{24} = 0.5\,\text{mol}\).

Step 2 — Ratio from equation: 2 mol Mg : 2 mol MgO → 1:1 ratio, so moles of MgO = 0.5 mol.

Step 3 — Mass of MgO: \(M_r(\text{MgO}) = 24 + 16 = 40\,\text{g/mol}\). Mass \(= 0.5 \times 40 = 20\,\text{g}\).

Limiting Reactants

In most reactions, one reactant runs out before the others. The limiting reactant determines the maximum amount of product. To identify it: calculate the moles of each reactant and compare to the stoichiometric ratio. Whichever reactant would be exhausted first is the limiting reactant; the other is in excess.

Key Fact

The limiting reactant is the one that runs out first. The amount of product formed is always calculated from the moles of the limiting reactant, not the excess reactant.

Percentage Yield

In practice, reactions rarely produce the theoretical maximum amount of product. Some product may be lost during transfer between vessels, some reactions may not go to completion, or unwanted side reactions may occur. The percentage yield compares the actual yield to the theoretical maximum:

$$\text{percentage yield} = \frac{\text{actual yield}}{\text{theoretical yield}} \times 100$$

Industrial chemists aim to maximise percentage yield to reduce waste and cost. Factors lowering yield include incomplete reactions, reversible reactions that reach equilibrium before completion, and losses during filtration or evaporation.

Q: A reaction has a theoretical yield of 50 g of aspirin. The chemist isolates 38 g. Calculate the percentage yield.

\(\text{percentage yield} = \frac{38}{50} \times 100 = 76\%\)

In an industrial context, a 76% yield would be assessed against the cost of raw materials and any waste disposal requirements before deciding if the process is commercially viable.

Atom Economy

Atom economy measures how efficiently a reaction converts reactants into the desired product. Unlike percentage yield (which measures what you got versus what you could get), atom economy is a property of the reaction equation itself:

$$\text{atom economy} = \frac{\text{sum of } M_r \text{ of desired products}}{\text{sum of } M_r \text{ of all products}} \times 100$$

A reaction where all atoms end up in the desired product has an atom economy of 100%. Addition reactions (where everything combines into one product) are ideal. Reactions that produce many by-products have low atom economy and generate chemical waste — an important issue in green chemistry and industrial sustainability.

Key Fact

Atom economy = (\(M_r\) of useful products ÷ \(M_r\) of all products) × 100. High atom economy is desirable — less waste, lower cost, more sustainable. A 100% atom economy means every atom of reactant ends up in the desired product.
lessons.exam_tip_html: The most common calculation error on moles questions is forgetting to divide mass by \(M_r\) — instead students just write down the mass. Always state the equation, substitute values, and give a final answer with units. For percentage yield: the theoretical yield must be calculated via balanced equation first, then divide actual by theoretical and multiply by 100. For atom economy: use the balanced equation and the \(M_r\) values of products only — not reactants. In 6-mark 'describe a method' questions on making a salt, examiners explicitly look for: independent variable, dependent variable, control variables, repeats, and how data will be analysed — missing any of these caps the mark.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • One mole = 6.02 × 10²³ particles. Moles = mass ÷ molar mass (\(M_r\)). \(M_r\) is found by adding up relative atomic masses for all atoms in the formula.
  • Balanced equations give molar ratios. The limiting reactant runs out first and determines the theoretical yield. Percentage yield = (actual ÷ theoretical) × 100.
  • Atom economy = (\(M_r\) of desired products ÷ \(M_r\) of all products) × 100. High atom economy means less waste — important for industrial sustainability and green chemistry.

lessons.title: Reactivity, Metal Extraction and Alloys
lessons.description: Reactivity series, displacement reactions, redox, metal extraction by reduction or electrolysis, and alloy properties.
lessons.content_html:
The Reactivity Series

Metals can be arranged in order of their chemical reactivity — this is called the reactivity series. From most to least reactive: potassium (K), sodium (Na), calcium (Ca), magnesium (Mg), aluminium (Al), carbon (C), zinc (Zn), iron (Fe), hydrogen (H), copper (Cu), silver (Ag), gold (Au). Carbon and hydrogen are included as non-metal reference points.

A more reactive metal will displace a less reactive metal from a solution of its compound. For example, iron displaces copper from copper(II) sulfate solution:

$$Fe + CuSO_4 \rightarrow FeSO_4 + Cu$$

The solution changes from blue to colourless, and a copper-coloured solid forms on the iron. This is evidence that a displacement reaction has occurred.

Key Fact

Reactivity series (most → least reactive): K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, C, Zn, Fe, H, Cu, Ag, Au. A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its compound. Metals above carbon must be extracted by electrolysis; those below carbon can be extracted by reduction with carbon.

Oxidation and Reduction (Redox)

Displacement reactions are redox reactions — one species is oxidised while another is reduced. The memory aid OIL RIG helps keep the definitions straight: Oxidation Is Loss (of electrons), Reduction Is Gain (of electrons).

In the iron/copper sulfate displacement reaction: iron atoms lose electrons to become \(Fe^{2+}\) ions — iron is oxidised. Copper(II) ions gain electrons to become copper atoms — copper is reduced.

Key Fact

OIL RIG — Oxidation Is Loss of electrons, Reduction Is Gain. In displacement reactions, the more reactive metal (higher in the series) is oxidised; the less reactive metal ion is reduced. Both changes happen simultaneously.

Extracting Metals from Their Ores

Most metals are found in the Earth's crust combined with other elements in ores. The method of extraction depends on the metal's position in the reactivity series:

  • Metals less reactive than carbon (e.g. iron, zinc, copper) — extracted by reduction with carbon. Carbon (or carbon monoxide) is more reactive than these metals under smelting conditions, so it removes the oxygen from the metal oxide.
  • Metals more reactive than carbon (e.g. aluminium, sodium, potassium) — must be extracted by electrolysis. This requires large amounts of electricity, making it much more expensive.

Iron is extracted from iron(III) oxide (\(Fe_2O_3\)) in a blast furnace. Coke (carbon) burns in hot air to form carbon dioxide, which then reacts with more coke to form carbon monoxide (CO). The carbon monoxide reduces the iron oxide:

$$Fe_2O_3 + 3CO \rightarrow 2Fe + 3CO_2$$

Limestone (\(CaCO_3\)) is added to remove acidic silicon dioxide impurities as liquid slag (calcium silicate), which is tapped off separately from the molten iron.

Rusting and Corrosion

Rusting occurs when iron or steel is exposed to both water and oxygen. The overall reaction produces hydrated iron(III) oxide (rust). Rusting is an oxidation process — iron is oxidised. Preventing rusting is commercially vital: methods include galvanising (zinc coating), painting, oiling, or using a sacrificial metal (attaching a more reactive metal that corrodes preferentially).

Alloys

A pure metal has a regular lattice of identical atoms that can slide over each other easily, making the metal soft. An alloy contains atoms of different sizes, which distort the lattice and make it harder for layers to slide. This makes alloys harder and stronger than the pure metals they contain.

Steel: iron + carbon (and sometimes other metals). Low-carbon steel is malleable; high-carbon steel is harder and more brittle; stainless steel (iron + chromium + nickel) is corrosion-resistant.

Bronze: copper + tin. Harder than copper alone; used for statues, bells and bearings.

Brass: copper + zinc. Harder than copper; used for musical instruments and decorative fittings.

Gold alloys (carat gold): pure gold is too soft for jewellery; it is alloyed with silver or copper. 18-carat gold contains 18 parts gold in 24 parts alloy (75% gold).

Key Fact

Alloys are harder than pure metals because the different-sized atoms disrupt the regular metallic lattice, preventing layers from sliding easily over each other.

Electroplating uses electrolysis to deposit a thin layer of metal onto an object. The object to be plated acts as the cathode (negative electrode), the plating metal acts as the anode (positive electrode), and both are placed in a solution containing ions of the plating metal. Metal ions are reduced at the cathode and deposited onto the object; the anode gradually dissolves to replenish the ions. Applications include chrome plating of car parts, silver plating of cutlery, and tin plating of steel cans.
lessons.exam_tip_html: OIL RIG is essential for redox questions — examiners want the electron transfer stated explicitly, not just 'iron lost electrons' without saying whether that is oxidation or reduction. For extraction questions: always check the metal's position relative to carbon — if it is above carbon it needs electrolysis, if below it can be reduced. For alloy questions: the key word is 'distort the lattice' — saying layers cannot 'slide' without explaining the different atomic sizes earns fewer marks. Electroplating and galvanising are Triple-only topics (not in Combined Science) — in your exam, these will be worth focused marks if they appear.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Reactivity series (K to Au): a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its compound. OIL RIG — the more reactive metal is oxidised (loses electrons), the less reactive metal ion is reduced (gains electrons).
  • Metals below carbon in the reactivity series are extracted by reduction with carbon (e.g. iron in the blast furnace). Metals above carbon (e.g. aluminium) need electrolysis — more expensive due to high electricity use.
  • Alloys are harder than pure metals because atoms of different sizes distort the lattice, preventing layers sliding. Rusting needs both water and oxygen; galvanising (zinc coating) and electroplating are protective methods.

lessons.title: Acids, pH and Making Salts
lessons.description: Acid-base reactions, the pH scale, neutralisation, preparation of pure dry salts and titration calculations.
lessons.content_html:
Acids, Bases and the pH Scale

An acid is a substance that produces hydrogen ions (\(H^+\)) when dissolved in water. A base is a substance that neutralises an acid. An alkali is a soluble base — it produces hydroxide ions (\(OH^-\)) when dissolved in water.

The pH scale runs from 0 (most acidic) to 14 (most alkaline), with 7 being exactly neutral. pH is measured using universal indicator (which changes colour) or a pH probe (which gives a precise digital reading).

Key Fact

Acids: produce \(H^+\) ions, pH 0–6. Neutral: pH 7. Alkalis: produce \(OH^-\) ions, pH 8–14. The neutralisation reaction: \(H^+ + OH^- \rightarrow H_2O\).

Neutralisation Reactions

Neutralisation occurs when an acid reacts with a base, producing a salt and water. The key reaction types are:

  • Acid + metal → salt + hydrogen gas. E.g. \(Mg + H_2SO_4 \rightarrow MgSO_4 + H_2\)
  • Acid + metal oxide → salt + water. E.g. \(CuO + H_2SO_4 \rightarrow CuSO_4 + H_2O\)
  • Acid + metal hydroxide → salt + water. E.g. \(NaOH + HCl \rightarrow NaCl + H_2O\)
  • Acid + metal carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide. E.g. \(CaCO_3 + 2HCl \rightarrow CaCl_2 + H_2O + CO_2\)

The name of the salt produced depends on the acid used: hydrochloric acid (HCl) makes chlorides, sulfuric acid (\(H_2SO_4\)) makes sulfates, and nitric acid (\(HNO_3\)) makes nitrates.

Key Fact

HCl → chlorides. \(H_2SO_4\) → sulfates. \(HNO_3\) → nitrates. Salt name = metal name + acid ending. Example: sodium + sulfuric acid → sodium sulfate.

Making Pure Dry Salts

To make copper(II) sulfate crystals from copper(II) oxide and sulfuric acid (a core practical):

  1. Warm dilute sulfuric acid in a beaker.
  2. Add excess copper(II) oxide (black powder) and stir until no more dissolves — the excess ensures all acid is used up.
  3. Filter the mixture to remove the excess copper(II) oxide.
  4. Evaporate the blue filtrate gently until crystals begin to form, then leave to crystallise fully.
  5. Pat the blue crystals dry with filter paper.

The independent variable is the amount of acid used; the thermometer measures temperature (it does not control it — the water bath controls temperature).

Some salts are insoluble and cannot be made by neutralisation. They are made by precipitation: mix two solutions whose ions react to form the insoluble salt. For example, to make barium sulfate: mix barium chloride solution with sodium sulfate solution — barium sulfate precipitates immediately. Filter, wash with distilled water and dry.

$$BaCl_2 + Na_2SO_4 \rightarrow BaSO_4 + 2NaCl$$

Titration

Titration is used to find the exact volume of acid needed to neutralise a known volume of alkali (or vice versa). The apparatus required includes a burette (to deliver the acid) and a pipette (to measure the exact volume of alkali). An indicator such as phenolphthalein or methyl orange shows when the endpoint is reached.

1. Rinse the burette with the acid solution, then fill it and record the initial reading to 0.05 cm³. 2. Use the pipette to measure an exact volume of alkali into a conical flask; add a few drops of indicator. 3. Add the acid from the burette drop by drop, swirling the flask. As the endpoint approaches, add half-drops. 4. Stop when the indicator changes colour permanently. Record the final burette reading. 5. Calculate the volume added (titre = final − initial). Repeat until two titres agree within 0.10 cm³; these are concordant results. Average the concordant results.

From a titration, use: \(n = c \times V\) where \(n\) = moles, \(c\) = concentration (mol/dm³), \(V\) = volume (dm³). Convert cm³ to dm³ by dividing by 1000.

Example: 25.0 cm³ of NaOH solution of concentration 0.10 mol/dm³ required 20.0 cm³ of HCl solution. Find the concentration of the HCl.

Moles NaOH \(= 0.10 \times 0.025 = 0.0025\) mol. From NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O, the ratio is 1:1, so moles HCl = 0.0025 mol. Concentration HCl \(= \frac{0.0025}{0.020} = 0.125\) mol/dm³.

A key distinction for the exam is between strong and weak acids: strength refers to the degree of ionisation in water, not concentration. A concentrated weak acid like ethanoic acid has a lower pH than a dilute weak acid, but both ionise only partially. When making soluble salts by neutralisation, use an indicator to find the exact equivalence point; when using an insoluble base, add excess and then filter to remove it — no indicator is needed because the excess base is simply removed by filtration.
lessons.exam_tip_html: On 6-mark 'describe a method' questions for making a soluble salt, examiners want: (1) add excess insoluble base to the acid; (2) filter to remove excess solid; (3) evaporate gently and crystallise. Crucially, a thermometer in the experiment measures temperature — the water bath controls it. Mixing these up is the most common mark loss in core practical questions. For titration calculations: always convert cm³ to dm³ before using \(n = c \times V\). Concordant results means two titres that agree within 0.10 cm³ — the anomalous (rough) result is excluded from the average.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Acids produce H⁺ ions (pH below 7); alkalis produce OH⁻ ions (pH above 7). Neutralisation: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O. HCl gives chlorides, H₂SO₄ gives sulfates, HNO₃ gives nitrates.
  • Soluble salts: add excess insoluble base to acid, filter, evaporate, crystallise. Insoluble salts: mix two solutions → precipitation, filter, dry.
  • Titration uses a burette and pipette to find exact volumes at neutralisation. Calculation: moles = concentration × volume (dm³). Average concordant titres only.

lessons.title: Electrolysis and Electrolytic Processes
lessons.description: Why electrolysis decomposes ionic compounds, half-equations, aluminium extraction and the copper sulfate core practical.
lessons.content_html:
What Is Electrolysis?

Electrolysis is the process of using an electric current to break down an ionic compound. The compound being broken down is called the electrolyte, and it must be either molten or dissolved so that the ions are free to move.

The electrolyte is connected to two solid conductors called electrodes. The cathode is the negative electrode; the anode is the positive electrode. The memory aid PANIC helps: Positive Anode, Negative Is Cathode.

Key Fact

Electrolysis: positive ions (cations) move to the cathode (negative) and gain electrons — this is reduction. Negative ions (anions) move to the anode (positive) and lose electrons — this is oxidation. PANIC: Positive Anode, Negative Is Cathode.

Electrolysis of Molten Ionic Compounds

When a molten ionic compound is electrolysed, only the ions from that compound are present. For molten lead(II) bromide (\(PbBr_2\)):

  • Cathode: \(Pb^{2+}\) ions gain electrons → lead metal deposited. \(Pb^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow Pb\)
  • Anode: \(Br^-\) ions lose electrons → bromine gas released. \(2Br^- \rightarrow Br_2 + 2e^-\)

These equations showing what happens at each electrode are called half-equations. The electrons lost at the anode must equal the electrons gained at the cathode.

Electrolysis of Aqueous Solutions

When an ionic compound is dissolved in water, \(H^+\) and \(OH^-\) ions from water are also present. This means there is competition at each electrode between different ions:

At the cathode:

  • If the metal cation is less reactive than hydrogen (e.g. Cu²⁺, Ag⁺) → the metal is deposited.
  • If the metal cation is more reactive than hydrogen (e.g. Na⁺, Zn²⁺) → hydrogen gas is produced instead.

At the anode:

  • If a halide ion is present (Cl⁻, Br⁻, I⁻) → the halogen is produced (e.g. chlorine gas).
  • If no halide is present → oxygen is produced from the discharge of \(OH^-\) ions.

Aluminium Extraction by Electrolysis

Aluminium is too reactive to be extracted by reduction with carbon, so it is extracted by electrolysis of molten aluminium oxide (\(Al_2O_3\)).

Pure aluminium oxide has a very high melting point (over 2000 °C). To reduce energy costs, it is dissolved in molten cryolite, which lowers the melting point to around 950 °C.

Key Fact

Aluminium extraction: electrolysis of \(Al_2O_3\) dissolved in molten cryolite (lowers melting point). At cathode: \(Al^{3+} + 3e^- \rightarrow Al\). At anode: oxygen released reacts with the carbon anodes, burning them away — they need regular replacement.

Cathode (reduction): \(Al^{3+} + 3e^- \rightarrow Al\)

Anode (oxidation): \(2O^{2-} \rightarrow O_2 + 4e^-\)

The oxygen produced at the anode reacts with the carbon (graphite) anodes at high temperature, forming carbon dioxide. This means the anodes gradually burn away and must be replaced regularly — a significant running cost.

Core Practical: Electrolysis of Copper Sulfate Solution

This core practical investigates the electrolysis of aqueous copper sulfate solution, comparing the effect of inert electrodes (carbon) versus active electrodes (copper).

With inert (carbon) electrodes:

  • Cathode: copper metal deposits (Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu). The cathode gains mass.
  • Anode: oxygen gas is produced (no halide present). The copper sulfate solution gradually becomes paler as Cu²⁺ ions are removed.

With copper electrodes (active):

  • Cathode: copper still deposits — cathode gains mass.
  • Anode: the copper anode dissolves (Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻). The anode loses mass. The Cu²⁺ concentration in solution remains roughly constant, making this the basis of copper purification and electroplating.

To test the gas at the anode: a glowing splint would relight if it were oxygen. To test for copper, observe the reddish-brown deposit at the cathode. Weigh the electrodes before and after to quantify mass changes.

Common Misconceptions and Exam Pitfalls

A frequent error is assuming that the positive electrode always produces oxygen — this only applies when no halide ions (such as chloride) are present in solution. When chloride ions are present in higher concentration, chlorine gas forms at the anode instead. Likewise, students sometimes confuse electrolytic cells with electrochemical cells: in an electrolytic cell, electrical energy is put in to drive a non-spontaneous chemical change, whereas in a galvanic cell, chemical energy is converted out to electrical energy. Always identify the type of electrode material and the ions present in solution before predicting products.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For half-equations, examiners check: (1) correct formula for the product, (2) the correct number of electrons, (3) the equation is balanced for both atoms and charge. At the cathode, electrons are added to the left side (reduction); at the anode, electrons appear on the right side (oxidation). PANIC helps: Positive Anode, Negative Is Cathode. For aqueous electrolysis questions, state the discharge rule clearly: at the cathode, hydrogen is produced if the metal is more reactive than hydrogen; at the anode, the halogen is discharged if a halide is present, otherwise oxygen. In the core practical on electrolysis of copper sulfate, using copper electrodes changes the outcome — the copper anode dissolves and replenishes the Cu²⁺ in solution rather than depositing copper, so the solution concentration stays roughly constant. Inert electrodes (carbon/platinum) give pure copper depositing at the cathode and oxygen at the anode.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Electrolysis breaks down ionic compounds using electricity. Positive ions move to the cathode (reduction); negative ions move to the anode (oxidation). PANIC: Positive Anode, Negative Is Cathode.
  • In aqueous solutions: cathode produces the metal (if less reactive than H) or hydrogen gas; anode produces a halogen (if halide present) or oxygen. Aluminium is extracted by electrolysis of Al₂O₃ dissolved in molten cryolite to lower the melting point.
  • The core practical electrolysing copper sulfate solution with inert electrodes deposits copper at the cathode and releases oxygen at the anode. With copper electrodes, the anode dissolves to replenish Cu²⁺ ions — the basis of electroplating.

lessons.title: Energy Changes and Reaction Profiles
lessons.description: Exothermic and endothermic reactions, bond energies, reaction profiles and activation energy.
lessons.content_html:
Energy in Chemical Reactions

All chemical reactions involve energy changes. When chemical bonds are broken, energy must be absorbed; when new bonds are formed, energy is released. The overall energy change depends on the balance between these two processes. If more energy is released than absorbed, the reaction is exothermic. If more energy is absorbed than released, it is endothermic.

Key Fact

Bond breaking is always endothermic (energy absorbed); bond making is always exothermic (energy released). The overall reaction type depends on which process releases or absorbs more energy.

Exothermic Reactions

In an exothermic reaction, the energy released when new bonds form is greater than the energy needed to break the original bonds. This surplus energy is transferred to the surroundings as heat, so the temperature of the surroundings rises. Everyday examples include combustion (burning fuels), neutralisation reactions between acids and alkalis, and the oxidation of metals. Hand warmers contain iron powder that reacts exothermically with oxygen from the air, steadily releasing warmth.

When methane burns in oxygen, new C—O and H—O bonds form in the products carbon dioxide and water. These new bonds release more energy than is needed to break the original C—H and O=O bonds. The equation is:

$$CH_4 + 2O_2 \rightarrow CO_2 + 2H_2O$$

The reaction is strongly exothermic — this is why burning fuels release heat and light.

Endothermic Reactions

In an endothermic reaction, the energy needed to break bonds in the reactants is greater than the energy released when new bonds form. Energy is therefore absorbed from the surroundings and the temperature falls. Thermal decomposition reactions are typically endothermic — for example, heating copper carbonate:

$$CuCO_3 \rightarrow CuO + CO_2$$

Sports injury cold packs exploit this principle: ammonium nitrate dissolves endothermically in water, absorbing heat from the injured area and producing an immediate cooling effect.

Key Fact

Exothermic: temperature of surroundings rises (e.g. combustion, neutralisation, hand warmers). Endothermic: temperature of surroundings falls (e.g. thermal decomposition, dissolving ammonium nitrate, cold packs).

Reaction Profiles

A reaction profile (also called an energy profile diagram) shows the energy of the system as reactants are converted to products. The vertical axis shows energy; the horizontal axis shows the ‘progress of reaction’ (sometimes called the reaction coordinate). Every reaction profile has a ‘hump’ — reactants must reach the top of this energy barrier before products can form.

Exothermic profile: The reactants start at a higher energy level than the products. The difference in height between reactants and products is the energy released to surroundings (−ΔH). The ‘hump’ above the reactants represents the activation energy required to start the reaction.

Endothermic profile: The products sit at a higher energy level than the reactants. Energy has been absorbed from the surroundings (+ΔH). The activation energy is the height from the reactants up to the peak of the hump.

A catalyst lowers the height of the activation energy hump, allowing more collisions to be successful at the same temperature — this is shown on a profile as a lower peak, with the reactant and product energy levels unchanged.

Activation Energy

The activation energy is the minimum energy that particles must possess for a collision to result in a reaction. Even strongly exothermic reactions require an initial energy input to break the first bonds and get the reaction started — a match is needed to ignite methane gas, for example. On a reaction profile, activation energy is the vertical distance from the reactant energy level to the peak of the curve.

A catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy. On a reaction profile, this appears as a lower peak. The overall energy change (ΔH) between reactants and products remains identical; only the barrier height changes. This means more collisions at a given temperature have enough energy to react, so the rate increases.

Bond Energy Calculations

Every chemical bond has a characteristic bond energy (in kJ/mol). By summing the bond energies of all bonds broken in the reactants and all bonds made in the products, the overall energy change for a reaction can be calculated:

$$\Delta H = \text{Energy to break bonds} - \text{Energy released making bonds}$$

A positive ΔH means energy is absorbed overall (endothermic); a negative ΔH means energy is released overall (exothermic).

Calculate the energy change for: \(H_2 + Cl_2 \rightarrow 2HCl\)

Bond energies: H—H = 436 kJ/mol; Cl—Cl = 242 kJ/mol; H—Cl = 431 kJ/mol

Step 1 — bonds broken: 1 × H—H (436) + 1 × Cl—Cl (242) = 678 kJ/mol

Step 2 — bonds made: 2 × H—Cl (2 × 431) = 862 kJ/mol

Step 3 — overall change: \(\Delta H = 678 - 862 = -184\) kJ/mol

The negative value confirms the reaction is exothermic — 184 kJ/mol is released to the surroundings.

Key Fact

ΔH = energy to break bonds − energy released making bonds. Negative ΔH = exothermic (energy released); positive ΔH = endothermic (energy absorbed). Always include the sign and units (kJ/mol) in your answer.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In bond energy calculations, show your working in three labelled steps (bonds broken, bonds made, overall change) and include the sign: a positive ΔH is endothermic, a negative ΔH is exothermic. Missing units (kJ/mol) or the sign will cost a mark.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Exothermic reactions release energy to the surroundings (temperature rises); endothermic reactions absorb energy (temperature falls). Bond breaking is always endothermic; bond making is always exothermic.
  • Reaction profiles show the energy of reactants and products; the peak represents the transition state and the activation energy is the height from reactants to that peak.
  • Bond energy calculations: ΔH = energy to break bonds − energy released making bonds. Negative ΔH = exothermic; positive ΔH = endothermic.
